title: Why Bizkaiko Txakolina tastes the way it does

lede.text: Bizkaia has an Atlantic, humid, temperate climate, with cool summers and little sun. The wines are lower in alcohol than in nearby zones, and higher in acidity.

terms.text: A Berezia that fermented, and turned from must to wine, in wooden barrels of up to 600 litres.
A wine sold under one grape's name must contain at least 85% of a recommended variety.
A late-harvest wine from overripe grapes, with at least 12% alcohol and 60 to 150 g/l of sugar.
A sparkling wine, at 20 °C a pressure of at least 3 bar and at least 10% alcohol.

chapters.title: Hills between two valleys
paras: The zone is the province of Bizkaia. Any municipality can take part, if the Consejo Regulador and the authorities judge the land fit for the permitted grapes.
Mountain ranges of medium height, 100 to 1,000 m, run mostly northwest to southeast. There are two main valleys, of the Ibaizabal and the Butrón.

chapters.title: Wet, mild and short of sun
paras: The climate is Atlantic, humid and temperate. Rain averages 1,200 mm a year and falls on 157 days. The average temperature is 12.4 °C.
The main winds blow from the north and northwest, 39% of the time. They come off the sea, colder and full of moisture. Vineyards therefore sit on slopes sheltered from them.
Humidity averages 82% over the year, and stays high in summer. The sun shines 1,710 hours a year. There are 145 overcast days and only 47 clear ones.
Summers are cool and mild, because the sea is close. The grapes ripen slowly.
September is different. A foehn effect makes it warmer and drier, more like summer. This decides the final ripening of the grapes.

chapters.title: South-facing slopes, grassed rows
paras: Vineyards are usually on slopes that face south. The slopes are moderate, so machines can work them.
Rain on 157 days a year gives the vines a regular supply of water. Grass or other cover can grow between the rows. That helps control vigour, and it keeps and improves the soil.

chapters.title: Hondarrabi Zuri and a bitter finish
paras: The main white grape is Hondarrabi Zuri. The main red is Hondarrabi Beltza. Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia (Petit Courbu) is also recommended. Other varieties are allowed, with limits.
A wine sold under one grape's name must use a recommended grape for at least 85% of the blend.
Yields are capped at 11,500 kg per hectare for white grapes and 9,500 kg for red.

The wines are dry. The minimum strength is 10.5% in a standard wine. Average strength is usually 10.5% to 11.5%. That is clearly lower than in nearby zones, because of the humid Atlantic climate with cool summers.
The cool summers and low sun leave less sugar and more acidity than in sunnier zones. Notes of white fruit, citrus and herbs go with this acidity.
The aroma is of medium intensity but very complex, from the grapes and slow ripening. A bitter finish is typical of Hondarrabi Zuri and Hondarrabi Zuri Zerratia.
